name: Karl Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the construction and hospitality team at a regional firm, about sixty people in a business park off the ring road. My clients are building contractors and restaurants, and I prepare their year-end accounts and the directors' personal tax returns. A normal day is chasing a builder for his van invoices, reconciling a restaurant's card takings, then drafting a return for Deborah, my manager, to review. I like the clients, they're real people with dust on their boots. What wears me out is chasing paperwork that should've come in months ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask a chatbot to summarise a VAT rule before I look it up properly, or to tidy an email to a client who's annoyed. Some of the team use it loads, some never touch it. I'm in the middle, I use it when I've seen it work for someone else first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and not much more. At football on Thursday I'd tell Tomasz from work that he can stop sending me articles about robots. Online I'd probably not bother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be fine for the job, but it doesn't help with what's actually on my mind. Ana and I are saving for a flat deposit and rents keep going up, three-fifty more a year on our last renewal. And two of my builders are struggling with late payments from big contractors, so if they go bust, I lose clients and maybe the firm looks at the team size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, pass my next exam in June, and keep putting four hundred a month into the deposit pot. I'd keep using the chatbot for the odd rule summary. And I'd keep my emergency savings separate, about four months, which Ana insists on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit of background worry about money and the builders, the normal kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if two builders go bust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Directly, not much, I'd get other files. Deborah's already warned us. Our team's targets are on fees, and construction is a hard sector this year. The newest junior is the one moved or not replaced. And that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long until you can buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two more years if nothing goes wrong. We've got about nine thousand in the pot. Ana's a dental hygienist and her pay's steady, which helps.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and not much more.
I'd tell Tomasz at football to **stop sending articles** about robots.
think: The **flat deposit** and rising rent are what's actually on my mind.
Builders **going bust** could shrink our team, starting with me.
do: Keep putting **£400 a month** into the deposit pot.
Keep **four months** of emergency savings separate, as Ana insists.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with normal background worry about money.
S0.quote: Our team's targets are on fees, and construction is a hard sector this year. The newest junior is the one moved or not replaced.
fieldNote: He feels secure in the job but carries **ordinary pressures**: rent and a deposit.
His clients' **late payments** are a real threat to his team, separate from AI.
He uses AI **after others prove it**, sitting firmly in the middle.

steps.text: Put £400 a month into the flat deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, so adapt, but let's not pretend it's painless. At work I'd say we need a proper plan for juniors. Online I'd share something balanced, not the doom stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits me. Drafting accounts and checking returns is what the card describes, and that's most of my day. The firm would keep the clients, keep Deborah and the seniors, and need fewer people like me. I'd probably survive the first round but not be sure about the second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Deborah to put me on whatever AI the firm brings in, early, so I'm one of the people who knows it. I'd push the flat purchase back a year and keep the deposit in savings, so we're not stuck with a mortgage if I'm cut. And I'd start looking at in-house roles at the bigger construction companies, where the job is closer to site costs and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the not knowing which round I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana about pushing the flat back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's a year, not forever. A mortgage on one salary would scare me more than renting for another year. She'd be disappointed, she's already looking at kitchens online. But she'd agree, she's more careful than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why in-house at a construction company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the job there includes walking round sites, arguing about variations with the site manager, that kind of thing. It's harder to hand to software when half of it's standing in mud. And I know the trade from my clients.

say: I'd say adapt, but **don't pretend** it's painless.
I'd ask for a proper **plan for juniors** at the firm.
think: Drafting and checking returns is **most of my day**, so it hits me.
I'd **survive the first round** of cuts but not be sure of the second.
do: Ask Deborah to put me on the **firm's AI tools** early.
Push the **flat purchase** back a year and keep the deposit.
Look at **in-house roles** at construction companies.
feel: **Anxious** about not knowing which round of cuts he's in.
S1.quote: A mortgage on one salary would scare me more than renting for another year.
fieldNote: He sees his own day as the **card's target** and expects rounds of cuts.
He'd **delay the flat** to avoid a mortgage on one income, a real family trade-off.
His move is toward **site-based** finance, betting that mud protects the job.

steps.text: Ask Deborah to join the firm's AI tool pilot
Push the flat purchase back by a year
Apply for in-house finance jobs at construction firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should slow it or cushion it. I'm not usually one for big statements, but two years is chaos. At work I'd say let's look after the clients through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd expect to be gone within a year of it arriving. All my work is thinking work. The construction companies keep site people for three more years, till the robots come, but their finance teams go with AGI like mine would. Ana cleans teeth, she's hands-on, so she has longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the flat plans completely and keep the nine thousand as savings, so with my four months we'd have nearly a year. I'd ask my builder clients about site work, labouring or helping a site manager, because the robots come later. And I'd cut the car, the football subs, anything that isn't rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground giving way. I'd be scared, and a bit ashamed, I think, going from accounts to labouring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mum was so proud when I got the degree, she framed the photo. Telling my mum I'm carrying plasterboard would be hard. Even though it's honest work and pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your builder clients would you call first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Marek, he runs a small renovation firm and he's always saying he needs someone who can read a spreadsheet and lift things. He'd laugh at me first. Then he'd probably say yes.

say: I'd say two years is **chaos** and the government should cushion it.
At work I'd say let's **look after clients** through it.
think: I'd expect to be **gone within a year** of AGI arriving.
Ana's **hands-on job** lasts longer than mine, till the robots come.
do: Cancel the flat and keep the **£9,000** as savings.
Ask builder clients about **site work** before robots arrive.
Cut the **car and football subs**, keeping only rent and food.
feel: **Scared**, and a bit **ashamed** of moving from accounts to labouring.
S2.quote: Telling my mum I'm carrying plasterboard would be hard. Even though it's honest work and pays the rent.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within a year and plans a hands-on bridge.
**Shame** about his mother's pride in the degree surfaces strongly here.
He uses the **robot gap** sensibly, through a builder client he already knows.

steps.text: Cancel the flat purchase plans with Ana
Keep the £9,000 deposit as an emergency fund
Ask Marek about site work at his renovation firm
Sell the car and drop football subs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to be sensible: train people, plan, don't panic. At work I'd push for us to learn the tools while we still can. Online I'd stay out of the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd get qualified and probably get a few good years. Then by 2031 the job probably goes. I'd want to be in a construction company by then, closer to site, so I've got the three robot years on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028, learn the firm's AI tools properly, and move in-house at a contractor around 2029. I'd keep saving the deposit but not buy, or buy something small we could cover on Ana's pay alone. And I'd do a short site safety course, so I could go on site if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but organised. Like knowing a deadline is coming, not knowing what's on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your manager about leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not early. I'd tell Deborah when I had an offer, she'd understand. She's said herself she's not sure what her own job looks like in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy something small. How small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe on the edge of town. A one-bed with a mortgage my partner could cover on her own is as far as I'd go before 2031. Ana would want two bedrooms for when we have kids. I'd say let's see what 2031 looks like first.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **be sensible** and not panic.
I'd push the team to **learn the tools** while we can.
think: I'd **qualify** and get a few good years before 2031.
Being **closer to site** gives me three robot years on top.
do: Qualify by 2028 and learn the **firm's AI tools**.
Do a short **site safety course** as a fallback.
feel: **Anxious but organised**, facing a deadline with an unknown after.
S3.quote: A one-bed with a mortgage my partner could cover on her own is as far as I'd go before 2031.
fieldNote: Five years becomes a **staged plan**: qualify, learn tools, move nearer site.
The flat is cut down to a **one-bed** that one income could cover.
He mentions his manager is **unsure** of her own job, a sign of pressure upward.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI accounting tools properly
Move in-house at a contractor around 2029
Take a short site safety course
Buy a one-bed Ana could afford alone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up, and people should use it rather than worry. At work I'd be the steady one. I don't think I'd say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is fine for my next few years. I'd buy the flat, qualify, get some experience, and I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. That's young enough to change, old enough to have savings. I'd probably still move toward construction finance, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat in the next two years like we planned. I'd use the AI tools once the team does, and get properly good at them. And around 2031 I'd move in-house at a contractor and maybe study quantity surveying part-time, which is half site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. Like knowing there's a big hill a long way ahead on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does quantity surveying mean, for someone who doesn't know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quantity surveying sits right between accounts and the hands-on stuff. Half of it is on site measuring things and arguing with builders. It's working out what a building should cost and checking what's been spent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, we'd still aim for about thirty. Ana's job would be fine for a while. We'd just want the flat paid down faster than normal.

say: I'd say ten years is a **decent run-up** to use, not worry about.
At work I'd be the **steady one**.
think: My **next few years** are fine, and I'd buy the flat.
At thirty-seven I'd be **young enough** to change, with savings.
do: Buy the **flat** in the next two years, as planned.
Use the **AI tools** once the team does.
Move to a contractor and study **quantity surveying** part-time around 2031.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, seeing a big hill far down the road.
S4.quote: Quantity surveying sits right between accounts and the hands-on stuff. Half of it is on site measuring things and arguing with builders.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him keep **family plans** on track, including the flat.
He aims at **quantity surveying**, a bridge between desk and site.
His mood eases because the **near-term job** looks safe.

steps.text: Buy the flat with Ana within two years
Learn the AI tools once the team adopts them
Move in-house at a building contractor

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd go from planning a flat to carrying plasterboard in about eighteen months. What would help is notice, real notice from the firm, and some kind of support while people retrain, so it's not a cliff. The government doesn't need to stop AI. The government needs to stop it being a cliff for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this is about pride. The money matters, but so does what you tell your family you do. That's harder to replace than a salary.

headlineQuote: The government doesn't need to stop AI. The government needs to stop it being a cliff for people like me.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old junior** on a regional firm's construction and hospitality team.
He uses AI **now and then**, once he's seen it work for others.
He and Ana are saving for a **flat deposit**, which every picture reshapes.
In faster pictures he'd bridge into **site work** through builder clients he knows.
**Pride** in his degree, and his mother's, runs under all his answers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, going from planning a flat to **labouring** in about eighteen months.
whatWouldHelp: **Real notice** from employers and support while people retrain.
A government that stops AI **being a cliff**, without stopping AI.
